Former defense attorney here. I'm not your attorney, and in any case I no longer practice, because the only true law is the law of power. This is not legal advice.

That being said ...

ACP (not to be confused with ICP, that's something totally different) is not a civil right. It is a rule of evidence.

If the State were somehow to acquire recordings of your conversations with your attorney and then try to introduce the substance of those conversations into evidence in a proceeding against you, your attorney could object to the State doing so, on the grounds that the conversation was protected by ACP. If the judge sustained your attorney's objection, the prosecutor would not be allowed to use that evidence against you.

If the State tried to start a proceeding against you based on conversations you had with your attorney, he could make the same objection.

However, you cannot bring a proceeding against the State because it violated your ACP. For one thing, it's not your case to bring, because ACP attaches to the attorney, not the client. You can't get in trouble for breaching ACP, but your attorney sure can. For another thing, as I said before, ACP is not a civil right, it is a rule of evidence; and you cannot bring a case against the State based on a violation of a rule of evidence.

In addition, just like every other situation, the State can always use "parallel construction" to begin or sustain its case against you. If, at any point, you said the same thing you said to your attorney to someone who was not your attorney, the State could (and most likely would) simply use that conversation as its evidence, instead of the ACP-protected one.

In summary: all phones are always listening, and ACP isn't as strong as you think, so don't say anything within earshot of a phone that you don't want held against you, because if the State wants to fuck you, it will, regardless of what the laws or rules say.
